title: Travel Agent: the 12-Part Framework Worked Through

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: OverviewA travel company wants an AI assistant for customers in three regions: AMER, EMEA and APJ. Five specialist agents handle search, booking, pricing, recommendations and travel policy. The first draft of the design ran every request through one shared cache, one retrieval stage, one LLM (large language model) step and one tool-calling stage, in that order. The hard constraint is that the diagram has to match how agents actually run. Each agent loops on its own, calls its own tools and finishes at its own pace, so a single shared pipeline either wastes work or holds it up. A review found five places where the draft broke that rule. This case takes the draft apart and redraws it. Rate limiting moves inside the gateway, the semantic cache is checked before any agent starts, each agent owns its retrieval and tool calls, and a synthesiser merges the results into one reply.

sections.title: The original, and what was wrong with it
sections.text: The original, and what was wrong with itThe first draft was a rigid pipeline. Five agents fanned out, and then all of their work squeezed through a single shared cache, a single retrieval stage, a single LLM (large language model) step and a single tool-calling stage, one after another. It needed five fixes. 1 · Rate limiting belongs inside the API gateway In the draft, Rate Limiter hung off the load balancer as its own box, side by side with the gateway. No line left it, so anything sent there went nowhere. Rate limiting is a rule the gateway applies to every request, not a route. A separate box implies a component, and rate limiting is a behaviour. 2 · The semantic cache is checked before any agent spawns The draft put the cache behind the five agents, so it was only consulted after they had all run. If a cache exists to cut LLM latency and cost, it must come before the costly work. Now the supervisor looks in the cache before doing anything else. On a hit, the answer goes back and no agent is spawned at all. In 12-part framework terms this is short-circuiting, and the placement decides whether the cache saves money or nothing. 3 · Retrieval is owned by each agent, not a shared stage A single compulsory retrieval box after all five agents made every agent query the vector DB, whether it needed to or not. Search and Recommendation do draw on regional travel content. Booking and Policy rarely do. In the fix, each agent calls retrieval itself, within its own loop, and only when its task calls for it. 4 · Tool calling, MCP and external APIs sit alongside the agents In the draft, all five agents passed in sequence through a shared LLM box, a shared tool-calling box and a shared MCP (Model Context Protocol) registry. That reads as though the request gets a single turn in total. Booking calls the Flight and Payment MCP servers during its own work; it cannot wait until four other agents finish. The redraw makes the LLM, the MCP registry, the external APIs and the vector DBs a shared backend that each agent calls on demand. 5 · A synthesiser agent replaces the missing aggregation step Nothing in the draft explained how five parallel results became a single reply. The flow carried on as one line, as though merging took care of itself. In the fix, a named Synthesiser Agent gathers the output of each agent that ran and settles any clash between them before the user sees anything. A Policy ruling that overrides a Booking choice is the classic example.

1 · Rate limiting belongs inside the API gateway

In the draft, Rate Limiter hung off the load balancer as its own box, side by side with the gateway. No line left it, so anything sent there went nowhere. Rate limiting is a rule the gateway applies to every request, not a route. A separate box implies a component, and rate limiting is a behaviour.

2 · The semantic cache is checked before any agent spawns

4 · Tool calling, MCP and external APIs sit alongside the agents

  • In the fix, a named Synthesiser Agent gathers the output of each agent that ran and settles any clash between them before the user sees anything.

sections.title: The corrected architecture
sections.text: The corrected architectureOn a cache hit, the user gets a reply and no agent starts. If it misses, the supervisor spawns only the agents this query calls for, and each one pulls from the shared backend only what its own task needs. The synthesiser merges their results into one answer, which is also saved to the cache.

sections.title: Data flow, in order
sections.text: Data flow, in order A user sends a request. Authentication confirms who they are, the load balancer picks an instance, and the gateway enforces rate limits before passing the request to the supervisor. First, the supervisor looks up the semantic cache. A hit returns at once, and no agent is spawned. On a miss, the supervisor starts only the agents this query calls for. Inside its own loop, an agent that needs context makes a tool call to the matching regional vector DB. In that same loop, it calls external APIs via the MCP registry. The synthesiser gathers the outputs, settles conflicts and writes one grounded reply. The user receives the reply, and a copy goes into the cache. Across the whole request, monitoring captures latency, token counts and a trace per agent.
sections.html:
Data flow, in order

  1. A user sends a request.
  2. Authentication confirms who they are, the load balancer picks an instance, and the gateway enforces rate limits before passing the request to the supervisor.
  3. First, the supervisor looks up the semantic cache.
  4. A hit returns at once, and no agent is spawned.
  5. On a miss, the supervisor starts only the agents this query calls for.
  6. Inside its own loop, an agent that needs context makes a tool call to the matching regional vector DB.
  7. In that same loop, it calls external APIs via the MCP registry.
  8. The synthesiser gathers the outputs, settles conflicts and writes one grounded reply.
  9. The user receives the reply, and a copy goes into the cache.
  10. Across the whole request, monitoring captures latency, token counts and a trace per agent.

sections.title: Trade-offs worth naming out loud
sections.text: Trade-offs worth naming out loudShared retrieval service vs per-agent RAG (retrieval-augmented generation). One shared retrieval layer gives you a single place to enforce data residency and guardrails, but every agent then depends on that one service. Per-agent retrieval matches how frameworks such as LangGraph and CrewAI wire tools to each agent, yet without governance you end up running several copies of the embedding stack. You can defend either choice. The real mistake is placing RAG beside the agents as if it were one of them; it is infrastructure, or a tool. Single agent vs multi-agent. Every extra agent adds coordination and a synthesis step you must pay for. Pay it when sub-tasks differ in their tools or guardrails, or must scale on their own. Booking and Policy plainly do. Semantic cache vs traditional cache. A traditional cache only hits on an exact repeat. A semantic cache also matches near-duplicates, so it can skip the entire fan-out rather than save a single call downstream. Global vs regional vector DBs. Stores per region make data-residency rules easier to meet and bring latency down. One global store is simpler to run and keeps regions consistent with each other.
sections.html:
Trade-offs worth naming out loud

Shared retrieval service vs per-agent RAG (retrieval-augmented generation). One shared retrieval layer gives you a single place to enforce data residency and guardrails, but every agent then depends on that one service. Per-agent retrieval matches how frameworks such as LangGraph and CrewAI wire tools to each agent, yet without governance you end up running several copies of the embedding stack. You can defend either choice. The real mistake is placing RAG beside the agents as if it were one of them; it is infrastructure, or a tool.

Single agent vs multi-agent. Every extra agent adds coordination and a synthesis step you must pay for. Pay it when sub-tasks differ in their tools or guardrails, or must scale on their own. Booking and Policy plainly do.

Semantic cache vs traditional cache. A traditional cache only hits on an exact repeat. A semantic cache also matches near-duplicates, so it can skip the entire fan-out rather than save a single call downstream.

Global vs regional vector DBs. Stores per region make data-residency rules easier to meet and bring latency down. One global store is simpler to run and keeps regions consistent with each other.

glossary.definition: retrieval-augmented generation: Fetch the relevant documents first, then have the model answer only from them.

sections.title: Interview lens
sections.text: Interview lensEach of the five fixes turns into a question you can put to any multi-agent diagram, your own included: Is each box a real component, or a policy that should live inside another one? Does the cache come ahead of the costly work it is meant to avoid? Are agents made to retrieve when they have no need to? Does every agent loop and call tools by itself, or must the whole request squeeze through a single shared stage? Where do the parallel results meet, and who settles disagreements between them?

Interview lens

Each of the five fixes turns into a question you can put to any multi-agent diagram, your own included:

  1. Is each box a real component, or a policy that should live inside another one?
  2. Does the cache come ahead of the costly work it is meant to avoid?
  3. Are agents made to retrieve when they have no need to?
  4. Does every agent loop and call tools by itself, or must the whole request squeeze through a single shared stage?
  5. Where do the parallel results meet, and who settles disagreements between them?

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.text: Key Takeaways The first draft was a rigid pipeline in which five agents squeezed through one shared cache, one retrieval stage, one LLM step and one tool-calling stage, and it needed five structural fixes. Rate limiting is a rule the API gateway applies to every request, not a separate box off the load balancer that leads nowhere. The supervisor looks in the semantic cache before doing anything else, and on a hit the answer goes back with no agent spawned. The cache's placement decides whether it saves money or nothing, because a cache consulted after all five agents have run avoids no work. A semantic cache also matches near-duplicate queries, so it can skip the entire fan-out rather than save a single call downstream. On a miss, the supervisor spawns only the specialists this query calls for, not all five by default. Each agent calls retrieval inside its own loop, because Search and Recommendation need regional travel content while Booking and Policy rarely do. The LLM, the MCP registry, the external APIs and the vector DBs form a shared backend that each agent calls on demand, so Booking reaches the Flight and Payment servers during its own work. A named synthesiser gathers the output of every agent that ran and settles clashes, such as a Policy ruling that overrides a Booking choice, before the user sees anything. The synthesised reply is written back to the cache so the next similar query can reuse it. Shared retrieval puts residency and guardrails in one place while per-agent retrieval risks duplicate embedding stacks, and the real mistake is drawing RAG as a peer of the agents. Extra agents add coordination and synthesis costs, which pay off only when sub-tasks differ in tools, guardrails or scaling, as Booking and Policy plainly do. Regional stores for AMER, EMEA and APJ ease data residency and cut latency, while one global store is simpler to run and keeps regions consistent. Monitoring spans every stage with latency, token usage, cache hit rate and a trace per agent.

glossary.definition: OpenID Connect: The login layer on top of OAuth. OAuth only says what an app may do; OIDC adds who the user is, as a signed ID token.
General Data Protection Regulation: The EU's data-privacy law: consent, the right to be forgotten, where data may live.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Reference design: the corrected version System design is the plan for how software parts work together to solve a business problem quickly, reliably and at scale. This page applies that plan to one sample system: an agentic AI travel assistant for customers in AMER, EMEA and APJ. It starts from a first-draft reference architecture and folds in five structural fixes that came out of two later reviews. What this is: A first-draft architecture for a travel-agent system laid it out as a rigid pipeline. Five agents fanned out, then all passed, in order, through one shared cache, one retrieval stage, one LLM (large language model) step and one tool-calling stage. An architecture review found four points where that order does not match how a multi-agent system runs. A separate blueprint, written independently, reached the same four fixes and added a fifth: a named Synthesiser Agent to fill the missing aggregation step. This page combines all five into one final architecture.
sections.html:
Reference design: the corrected version

  • System design is the plan for how software parts work together to solve a business problem quickly, reliably and at scale.
  • This page applies that plan to one sample system: an agentic AI travel assistant for customers in AMER, EMEA and APJ.
  • It starts from a first-draft reference architecture and folds in five structural fixes that came out of two later reviews.

What this is: A first-draft architecture for a travel-agent system laid it out as a rigid pipeline. Five agents fanned out, then all passed, in order, through one shared cache, one retrieval stage, one LLM (large language model) step and one tool-calling stage. An architecture review found four points where that order does not match how a multi-agent system runs. A separate blueprint, written independently, reached the same four fixes and added a fifth: a named Synthesiser Agent to fill the missing aggregation step. This page combines all five into one final architecture.

glossary.definition: large language model: The model that reads text and writes text — GPT, Claude, Llama. Powerful, but it will confidently make things up if you let it.

sections.title: What changed, and why
sections.text: What changed, and whyThe first draft needed five structural fixes. Four came from the architecture review and one from the earlier blueprint. 1 · Rate limiting moved inside the API Gateway In the first draft, Rate Limiter was a separate box off the load balancer, next to the Gateway, with nothing flowing out of it. It was a dead end. Rate limiting is a rule the Gateway enforces on every request, not a path a request takes. 2 · Semantic Cache checked before any agent spawns The cache used to come after all five agents had finished. A cache that is meant to cut LLM latency and cost can only do so if it sits ahead of the costly work. It is now the first thing the Supervisor checks, and on a hit the answer returns with no agent spawned. 3 · RAG owned by each agent, not a shared stage A single required retrieval box after all five agents made every agent hit the vector DB, even agents with no use for it. Search and Recommendation do need regional travel content. Booking and Policy seldom do. So each agent now calls retrieval for itself, when it needs to. 4 · Tool calling, MCP, and external APIs sit alongside the agents The draft pushed every agent through one shared LLM step, then a single Tool Calling step, then a single MCP (Model Context Protocol) Registry, as though the request had only one turn in total. The Booking Agent needs the Payment and Flight MCP servers while it is running, not after four unrelated agents have wrapped up. 5 · A Synthesiser Agent replaces the missing aggregation step The draft never said how five parallel outputs turn into one reply. It kept going as a single line, as if merging happened by itself. Now a named Synthesiser Agent combines the output of every agent that ran and settles conflicts between them before the user sees anything. A Policy decision that overrides a Booking choice is a typical case.
sections.html:
What changed, and why

The first draft needed five structural fixes. Four came from the architecture review and one from the earlier blueprint.

1 · Rate limiting moved inside the API Gateway

In the first draft, Rate Limiter was a separate box off the load balancer, next to the Gateway, with nothing flowing out of it. It was a dead end. Rate limiting is a rule the Gateway enforces on every request, not a path a request takes.

2 · Semantic Cache checked before any agent spawns

The cache used to come after all five agents had finished. A cache that is meant to cut LLM latency and cost can only do so if it sits ahead of the costly work. It is now the first thing the Supervisor checks, and on a hit the answer returns with no agent spawned.

3 · RAG owned by each agent, not a shared stage

A single required retrieval box after all five agents made every agent hit the vector DB, even agents with no use for it. Search and Recommendation do need regional travel content. Booking and Policy seldom do. So each agent now calls retrieval for itself, when it needs to.

4 · Tool calling, MCP, and external APIs sit alongside the agents

The draft pushed every agent through one shared LLM step, then a single Tool Calling step, then a single MCP (Model Context Protocol) Registry, as though the request had only one turn in total. The Booking Agent needs the Payment and Flight MCP servers while it is running, not after four unrelated agents have wrapped up.

5 · A Synthesiser Agent replaces the missing aggregation step
  • The draft never said how five parallel outputs turn into one reply.
  • It kept going as a single line, as if merging happened by itself.
  • Now a named Synthesiser Agent combines the output of every agent that ran and settles conflicts between them before the user sees anything.
  • A Policy decision that overrides a Booking choice is a typical case.

glossary.definition: Model Context Protocol: An open standard for plugging tools and data sources into an AI app, so each tool is written once and reused.

sections.title: Architecture
sections.text: ArchitectureThe components and the regional footprint match the first draft. The structure is what changes: a cache hit is now cheap, each agent uses its tools within its own loop, and all results pass through one accountable step before the reply leaves. Solid lines: the request path, and the agents, each running its own loop in parallel Dashed lines: the shared backend, called only when needed New in this version: the Synthesiser Agent A cache hit returns before the Supervisor spawns any agent. On a miss, the Supervisor spawns only the agents this query needs. Each of them calls the shared backend on its own (the Foundation LLM, the regional vector DBs, the MCP registry and the external APIs) for only what its task requires. The Synthesiser Agent then combines whatever ran into a single reply, and that reply is written back to the cache so the next similar query can reuse it.

sections.title: Data flow
sections.text: Data flowThe ten steps from the first draft, put in a new order so that the cache check comes first. A user sends a request from the web or mobile client. Authentication confirms the user's identity. The Load Balancer sends the request to a free API instance. The API Gateway enforces rate limits and hands the request to the Supervisor. Before making any decision about agents, the Supervisor checks the Semantic Cache. If the cache hits, the stored answer goes straight back and no agent is spawned at all. If it misses, the Supervisor spawns the specialised agents this query calls for (Search, Booking, Pricing, Recommendation, Policy). Each agent pulls the context it needs from the right regional Vector DB, using a tool call within its own loop. Each agent calls the external APIs it needs (flights, hotels, maps, payment) through the MCP Tool Registry, again within its own loop. The Synthesiser Agent gathers every agent's output, settles conflicts and writes one grounded reply. The user gets the final reply, and the answer is stored in the Semantic Cache so later queries can reuse it. Monitoring and logging record latency, token usage and per-agent traces for the whole request.
sections.html:
Data flow

The ten steps from the first draft, put in a new order so that the cache check comes first.

  1. A user sends a request from the web or mobile client.
  2. Authentication confirms the user's identity. The Load Balancer sends the request to a free API instance. The API Gateway enforces rate limits and hands the request to the Supervisor.
  3. Before making any decision about agents, the Supervisor checks the Semantic Cache.
  4. If the cache hits, the stored answer goes straight back and no agent is spawned at all.
  5. If it misses, the Supervisor spawns the specialised agents this query calls for (Search, Booking, Pricing, Recommendation, Policy).
  6. Each agent pulls the context it needs from the right regional Vector DB, using a tool call within its own loop.
  7. Each agent calls the external APIs it needs (flights, hotels, maps, payment) through the MCP Tool Registry, again within its own loop.
  8. The Synthesiser Agent gathers every agent's output, settles conflicts and writes one grounded reply.
  9. The user gets the final reply, and the answer is stored in the Semantic Cache so later queries can reuse it.
  10. Monitoring and logging record latency, token usage and per-agent traces for the whole request.

sections.title: Trade-offs worth naming out loud
sections.text: Trade-offs worth naming out loudThe contrasts an interviewer wants to hear you draw. Shared retrieval service vs. per-agent RAG (retrieval-augmented generation). A shared Vector DB layer puts data-residency and guardrail enforcement in one place, but it ties every agent to that single service. Retrieval per agent mirrors how LangGraph- and CrewAI-style frameworks attach tools, yet without governance it duplicates the embedding infrastructure. Both positions hold up. The real mistake is drawing RAG as a peer of the agents, when it is infrastructure or a tool. Single agent vs. multi-agent. Several agents bring coordination and synthesis costs. Those costs pay off when sub-tasks need their own tools, their own guardrails or their own scaling, which is plainly true of Booking and Policy here. Semantic cache vs. traditional cache. A semantic cache hits on near-duplicate queries as well as exact repeats. That is why it can skip the entire agent fan-out instead of saving a single call further down. Global vs. regional vector DBs. Stores per region (AMER/EMEA/APJ) make data-residency rules easier to meet and cut latency. A single global store is simpler to operate and keeps regions consistent with each other.
sections.html:
Trade-offs worth naming out loud

The contrasts an interviewer wants to hear you draw.

Shared retrieval service vs. per-agent RAG (retrieval-augmented generation). A shared Vector DB layer puts data-residency and guardrail enforcement in one place, but it ties every agent to that single service. Retrieval per agent mirrors how LangGraph- and CrewAI-style frameworks attach tools, yet without governance it duplicates the embedding infrastructure. Both positions hold up. The real mistake is drawing RAG as a peer of the agents, when it is infrastructure or a tool.

Single agent vs. multi-agent. Several agents bring coordination and synthesis costs. Those costs pay off when sub-tasks need their own tools, their own guardrails or their own scaling, which is plainly true of Booking and Policy here.

Semantic cache vs. traditional cache. A semantic cache hits on near-duplicate queries as well as exact repeats. That is why it can skip the entire agent fan-out instead of saving a single call further down.

Global vs. regional vector DBs. Stores per region (AMER/EMEA/APJ) make data-residency rules easier to meet and cut latency. A single global store is simpler to operate and keeps regions consistent with each other.

glossary.definition: retrieval-augmented generation: Fetch the relevant documents first, then have the model answer only from them.
